items.name: Hezekiah
items.subtitle: King of Judah
items.summary: Hezekiah ruled Judah during the Assyrian crisis and is remembered for religious reform, trust in God, and his confrontation with Sennacherib's empire.
quickFacts: Isaiah was active during Hezekiah's reign.
Sennacherib invaded Judah during Hezekiah's reign.
The Assyrian campaign against Judah is also known from ancient Assyrian records.
items.certaintyNote: Exact regnal chronology is debated; dates are approximate.

items.name: Sennacherib
items.subtitle: King of the Neo-Assyrian Empire
items.summary: Sennacherib was one of Assyria's most powerful rulers. His 701 BC campaign against Judah brought his forces into direct conflict with King Hezekiah.
quickFacts: Sennacherib made Nineveh a major royal center.
His records mention Hezekiah of Judah.
His palace displayed reliefs celebrating the conquest of Lachish.

sources.title: 2 Kings 18–19
sources.note: Biblical account of Sennacherib's campaign against Judah.

sources.title: Isaiah 36–37
sources.note: Parallel prophetic account of the Assyrian confrontation.

items.name: Isaiah
items.subtitle: Prophet of Judah
items.summary: Isaiah ministered in Judah across the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah and played a key role during the Assyrian crisis.
quickFacts: Isaiah's ministry crossed the reigns of four kings named in Isaiah 1:1.
He appears directly in the Hezekiah narrative.
His ministry took place during the rise of Assyrian power.

items.name: Siege of Lachish
items.subtitle: Assyrian campaign in Judah
items.summary: During Sennacherib's campaign against Judah, the fortified city of Lachish was attacked and captured before the confrontation over Jerusalem.
quickFacts: Lachish was one of Judah's major fortified cities.
The campaign occurred during Hezekiah's reign.
Ancient Assyrian reliefs portray the city's conquest.

sources.title: 2 Kings 18
sources.note: Places Sennacherib at Lachish during the campaign against Judah.

items.name: Lachish Reliefs
items.subtitle: Assyrian palace reliefs
items.summary: These carved palace panels depict the Assyrian conquest of Lachish and provide a rare visual window into warfare, prisoners, and royal propaganda from the biblical world.
quickFacts: The reliefs came from Sennacherib's palace at Nineveh.
They depict siege warfare and Judean captives.
They are now held by the British Museum.

items.name: Saul
items.subtitle: First king of Israel
items.summary: Saul, from the tribe of Benjamin, became Israel's first king. His reign includes wars with the Philistines, his troubled relationship with David, and his death at Mount Gilboa.
quickFacts: Saul was from the tribe of Benjamin.
Samuel anointed Saul as king.
Saul and his sons died after the battle at Mount Gilboa.
items.certaintyNote: Absolute dates for Saul's reign are uncertain.

items.name: David
items.subtitle: King of Israel and Judah
items.summary: David rose from shepherd and warrior to king, established Jerusalem as his royal center, and became the central royal figure in Israel's biblical tradition.
quickFacts: David first served in Saul's court.
Jerusalem became David's royal capital.
The biblical books of Samuel give the fullest narrative of his reign.
items.certaintyNote: The scale and political character of David's kingdom remain subjects of archaeological debate.

items.name: Solomon
items.subtitle: King of Israel
items.summary: Solomon succeeded David and is remembered for wisdom, international connections, major building projects, and construction of the First Temple in Jerusalem.
quickFacts: Solomon was a son of David.
The First Temple is attributed to his reign in the biblical account.
After Solomon, the kingdom divided.
items.certaintyNote: Precise absolute dates and the scale of Solomon's kingdom are debated.

items.name: Samuel
items.subtitle: Prophet and judge
items.summary: Samuel stands at the transition from Israel's judges to monarchy. He anointed Saul and later David and repeatedly confronted Israel's kings with prophetic authority.
quickFacts: Samuel's mother was Hannah.
Samuel anointed both Saul and David.
His life bridges the era of the judges and kings.

sources.title: 1 Samuel 1–25

items.name: Jerusalem
items.subtitle: Royal and religious center of Judah
items.summary: Jerusalem became David's royal center and later the site of Solomon's Temple. It remained the capital of Judah until Babylon captured and destroyed the city in the early sixth century BC.
quickFacts: David captured Jerusalem and made it his capital in the biblical narrative.
Solomon's Temple stood in Jerusalem.
Babylon destroyed Jerusalem during Zedekiah's reign.

items.name: Divided Kingdom
items.subtitle: Israel and Judah separate
items.summary: After Solomon's death, the biblical kingdom divided into a northern kingdom called Israel and a southern kingdom called Judah, shaping the political setting of the later kings and prophets.
quickFacts: Rehoboam ruled Judah.
Jeroboam I became king of the northern kingdom.
The division forms the background for many prophetic books.

sources.note: Primary biblical passage for this entry.

sources.title: 2 Chronicles 10

items.name: Rehoboam
items.subtitle: King of Judah
items.summary: Rehoboam, Solomon's son, ruled Judah when the northern tribes broke away and formed a separate kingdom under Jeroboam I.
quickFacts: Rehoboam was Solomon's son.
The kingdom divided early in his reign.
Jerusalem remained the capital of Judah.
items.certaintyNote: Regnal dates vary among chronological systems.

items.name: Jeroboam I
items.subtitle: First king of northern Israel
items.summary: Jeroboam I became the first ruler of the northern kingdom after the split from Rehoboam and established alternative worship centers at Bethel and Dan in the biblical account.
quickFacts: Jeroboam had previously served Solomon.
He ruled the northern kingdom of Israel.
Bethel and Dan became important royal cult centers.
items.certaintyNote: Regnal dates vary among chronological systems.

sources.title: 1 Kings 11–14

items.name: Ahab
items.subtitle: King of northern Israel
items.summary: Ahab ruled the northern kingdom during a period of regional conflict and appears prominently in the Elijah narratives. His dynasty was connected by marriage to Jezebel of Sidon.
quickFacts: Ahab was the son of Omri.
Jezebel was his queen.
Elijah confronted Ahab during his reign.

sources.title: 1 Kings 16–22
sources.note: Primary biblical passage for this entry.

items.name: Jezebel
items.subtitle: Queen of northern Israel
items.summary: Jezebel, a Phoenician princess married to Ahab, is a major royal figure in Kings and a central opponent in the Elijah narratives.
quickFacts: Jezebel was married to Ahab.
She was associated with Sidon and Phoenician royalty.
Her story intersects repeatedly with Elijah.

items.name: Elijah
items.subtitle: Prophet in northern Israel
items.summary: Elijah confronted Ahab and Jezebel, challenged Baal worship, and became one of the best-known prophets of the northern kingdom.
quickFacts: Elijah confronted the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel.
He challenged King Ahab over Naboth's vineyard.
Elisha became his prophetic successor.

items.name: Elisha
items.subtitle: Prophet in northern Israel
items.summary: Elisha succeeded Elijah and appears in narratives involving kings, warfare, healing, famine, and relations between Israel and neighboring Aram.
quickFacts: Elisha succeeded Elijah.
His ministry involved both ordinary families and kings.
His narratives frequently intersect with Israel's wars with Aram.

items.name: Mount Carmel Contest
items.subtitle: Elijah and the prophets of Baal
items.summary: The Mount Carmel narrative presents Elijah challenging prophets of Baal during Ahab's reign in a dramatic contest over whom Israel should worship.
quickFacts: The event occurs during Ahab's reign.
Elijah challenges prophets associated with Baal.
Mount Carmel lies near Israel's Mediterranean coast.

items.name: Assyrian Empire
items.subtitle: Dominant Near Eastern empire
items.summary: The Neo-Assyrian Empire became the dominant power of the ancient Near East, conquered the northern kingdom of Israel, and later invaded Judah during Hezekiah's reign.
quickFacts: Assyria conquered Samaria.
Sennacherib was one of its most famous kings.
Nineveh became a major Assyrian capital.

items.name: Fall of Samaria
items.subtitle: End of the northern kingdom
items.summary: Samaria fell to Assyria after a siege, bringing the northern kingdom of Israel to an end and transforming the political world inherited by Judah.
quickFacts: Samaria was the capital of the northern kingdom.
Assyria deported inhabitants after the conquest.
Judah survived as the remaining Israelite kingdom.
items.certaintyNote: The final conquest spans the transition between the reigns of Shalmaneser V and Sargon II.

items.subtitle: King of Judah
items.summary: Josiah is remembered for major religious reforms after a book of the law was found in the Temple. He later died after confronting Pharaoh Neco at Megiddo.
quickFacts: Josiah became king while still young.
His reign included a major reform movement.
He died after the confrontation at Megiddo.

quickFacts: Jeremiah began his ministry during Josiah's reign.
He warned repeatedly of Babylonian judgment.
His ministry continued through Jerusalem's fall.

quickFacts: Josiah died after the confrontation.
The event occurred at Megiddo.
Judah soon came under increasing pressure from Egypt and Babylon.

items.subtitle: King of Babylon
items.summary: Nebuchadnezzar II ruled Babylon during Judah's final years, captured Jerusalem, deported Judeans, and oversaw the destruction of the city and Temple.
quickFacts: Nebuchadnezzar ruled the Neo-Babylonian Empire.
Jerusalem fell during his reign.
Daniel's opening chapters are set in the Babylonian court.

items.name: Fall of Jerusalem
items.subtitle: Babylon captures Judah's capital
items.summary: After a prolonged Babylonian siege, Jerusalem was captured, the Temple and major buildings were burned, and the kingdom of Judah came to an end.
quickFacts: Zedekiah was Judah's final king before the city's fall.
The Temple was burned.
Many Judeans were deported to Babylon.

quickFacts: Deportations occurred in more than one wave.
Jeremiah wrote to exiles in Babylon.
Ezekiel's prophetic ministry began among exiles.

items.name: Babylonian Empire
items.subtitle: Neo-Babylonian Empire
items.summary: The Neo-Babylonian Empire replaced Assyria as the dominant Mesopotamian power and under Nebuchadnezzar II conquered Judah and Jerusalem.
quickFacts: Babylon succeeded Assyria as the region's dominant empire.
Nebuchadnezzar II was its most prominent biblical ruler.
The empire fell to Persia in 539 BC.

items.name: Isaiah
items.subtitle: Prophet of Judah
items.summary: Isaiah was a prophet in Judah whose ministry spanned the reigns of several kings, including Hezekiah. He warned of judgment, confronted the threat of Assyria, and delivered messages of hope and restoration.
quickFacts: Isaiah ministered during the reign of King Hezekiah.
He witnessed the Assyrian threat against Jerusalem.
The book of Isaiah contains messages of judgment, hope, and restoration.

items.name: Daniel
items.subtitle: Prophet in Babylon
items.summary: Daniel was taken from Judah to Babylon and served in the courts of powerful kings while remaining faithful to God. The book of Daniel records his interpretation of dreams, his survival in the lions' den, and visions concerning kingdoms and God's ultimate rule.
quickFacts: Daniel was taken to Babylon during the reign of King Nebuchadnezzar II.
He became known for wisdom and the interpretation of dreams.
Daniel served under both Babylonian and Medo-Persian rulers.
His story includes the famous account of Daniel in the lions' den.
items.certaintyNote: The historical setting is the Babylonian and early Persian periods, though scholars debate the dating and composition of the book of Daniel.
